title: Paul Graham and Mike Moritz on early-stage investing: build, be candid, skip forecasts
summary: At a revenue bootcamp fireside chat, Paul Graham explains how YC picks founders (people who build things for love, not proven résumés), why he ignores revenue forecasts, why founders should be candid with smart investors, and how to spot the next platform. Mike Moritz of Sequoia adds the VC view.

principles.text: Proven means evidence you love building: ask what they made outside school or work because they liked it.
principles.quote: the big question we ask is what have you made outside of school or work because you liked it? Because if you don't like it, you're not going to do well as a startup founder.

principles.text: Early on, ignore revenue forecasts; what matters is whether people will really want what you're building.
principles.quote: We have a don't ask, don't tell policy on revenue projections. We don't even ask.

principles.text: Show care rather than announce it; generic words like 'passion' set off the BS detector.
principles.quote: you shouldn't say the word passion. You should just seem like you care.

principles.text: With smart investors be candid, like telling a doctor your symptoms; they will spot a lie anyway.
principles.quote: the smarter the investor, the more you should just be candid.

principles.text: Best startup ideas are things the founders themselves want to use, or someone close to them wants.
principles.quote: It's ideal if they're building something they themselves want to use. The next best thing is something, you know, that someone very close to them, like their wife or sibling wants to use.

principles.text: Predict which platforms win by watching what hackers themselves use, because they build for what they own.
principles.quote: look for the platforms that hackers themselves use and those are the ones exciting things are going to happen to you
